concept.name: False discovery rate
concept.definition: The expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections in a multiple-testing procedure, FDR = E[V/R] (defined as 0 when R = 0), where V counts false positives among R rejections. Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) proposed controlling it as a less conservative alternative to familywise error rates.
concept.intuition: Instead of demanding zero chance of any false positive, accept that a small controlled fraction of your discoveries may be false, buying back the power to find real effects among many tests.
concept.mechanics: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure orders the p-values p_(1) <= ... <= p_(m), finds the largest k with p_(k) <= (k/m) q, and rejects hypotheses 1 through k; this controls the FDR at level q under independence (and under positive dependence).
concept.formula: FDR = E[V / max(R, 1)]; BH rejects H_(1),...,H_(k) where k = max{ i : p_(i) <= (i/m) q }.
concept.failure_modes: BH control can fail under strong arbitrary dependence among test statistics, requiring the much more conservative Benjamini-Yekutieli adjustment, and the FDR bounds a rate, not which specific rejections are false.
concept.misconceptions: That FDR control at 5% gives each rejected hypothesis a 5% chance of being false: it bounds the average proportion of false rejections across the whole rejection set.
concept.example: Screening 1,000 candidate alpha signals at FDR q = 0.10, the BH procedure rejects 40, and in expectation no more than about 4 of those are false positives.
